label: Conics and Their Duals
notes: This chapter, printed pages 145 through 166, treats a conic as a single algebraic object: a symmetric three by three matrix. From that one matrix flow the point equation, polar lines, tangents, the dual envelope, and a clean classification. Stress that the affine pictures are only inspection windows onto projective algebra.

label: A Conic as a Quadratic Form
notes: Define the conic as the zero set of the homogeneous quadratic form x transpose A x with A symmetric. Emphasize that only the symmetric part survives, that scaling A or x changes nothing projectively, and that homogenizing a familiar circle or ellipse equation immediately produces this matrix shape.

label: Reading the Matrix Entries
notes: Walk through which matrix entries are diagonal squares and which are the doubled mixed and linear terms. Point out that a point lies on the conic exactly when the form vanishes, and that the upper-left two by two block already hints at the affine type through its determinant sign.

label: Projective Classification
notes: State the central classification: rank and signature are the only projective invariants of a symmetric matrix, so every nondegenerate real conic is projectively equivalent to a single normal form. Contrast the full-rank cases with the rank-two line pairs and the rank-one double line, listing each signature.

label: All Nondegenerate Conics Agree
notes: Drive home that ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola differ only by how they meet the line at infinity, not as projective objects. A homography can carry any one to any other. The affine names are chart artifacts; the projective truth is one conic up to equivalence.

label: Poles and Polars
notes: Introduce polarity as the map sending a point x to the line A x. Define conjugacy through the symmetric pairing x transpose A y. Explain that the map is an involution when A is invertible, since the inverse matrix sends the polar line back to its pole. This duality is the engine of the chapter.

label: The Polar Dictionary
notes: Give the inside, on, and outside dictionary for an ellipse. A point on the conic has its tangent as polar. An exterior point has a polar secant cutting the conic at the two points where its tangents touch. An interior point has a polar that misses the real curve entirely. Tie each to the discriminant sign.

label: Tangents as Polars
notes: Show that the tangent at a conic point is precisely the polar of that point, because the line through it meets the conic in a double root. Then construct the two tangents from an exterior point as the joins to the two intersection points its polar carves out of the curve.

label: The Dual Conic
notes: Define the dual conic as the set of tangent lines, governed by the adjugate or inverse matrix through l transpose A inverse l equals zero. Stress the duality of viewpoint: the same conic is simultaneously a locus of points and an envelope of lines, and the tangent family wraps the curve.

label: Locus and Envelope Together
notes: Use the envelope picture to make the point-line symmetry concrete: dozens of tangent lines, none drawn on the curve, yet together they outline it. The dual conic A inverse lives in line space exactly as A lives in point space, and tangency is the bridge between the two.

label: Degenerate Conics and the Adjugate
notes: Treat degeneracy as legitimate projective content. A rank-two conic is a line pair whose adjugate stores its singular point; a rank-one double line has vanishing adjugate. This loss is why the chapter introduces primal-dual pairs, where a second matrix carries the tangent data the primal can no longer hold.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by collecting the dictionary: one symmetric matrix gives the point equation, sends points to polars, produces tangents, transforms by the inverse, classifies by rank and signature, and pairs with a dual through a product condition. Ask students to recite which matrix operation realizes each geometric act.
